unit.title: Prepare for oxyacetylene/metal arc welding processes

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to prepare, as a team leader, for oxy-acetylene and manual metal arc welding to a written procedure. You will learn to read and apply the WPS and check welders' qualifications, choose the process and consumables, plan a safe work area under a hot work permit, set up and check MMAW stations and oxy-acetylene equipment, work out and inspect joint fit-ups, control hydrogen and distortion, and keep the records a coded job needs.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers everything that happens **before the first production weld**: reading the procedure, choosing and checking the process and consumables, making the work area safe, setting up the oxy-acetylene and manual metal arc (MMAW) equipment, preparing and fitting the joints, and checking and recording that all of it is right.

At Level 2 you learned to prepare for your own work. At Level 3 you **plan and lead**: you prepare joints for a team, to a written welding procedure specification (WPS), on jobs that may be inspected against a code. You must be able to say **why** each step is done, work out the joint sizes, check other people's set-ups, and sign the records.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders moving into charge-hand or supervisor work in Jamaican fabrication shops, on construction sites, and in the maintenance departments of sugar, bauxite and water-supply plants.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Get the right WPS for each joint, read it, check that each welder is qualified for the job, and keep the WPS at the work place.
Plan the job and choose the process
Decide when oxy-acetylene, MMAW or another process suits the job, write a preparation plan, give out the roles and brief the team.
Do the risk assessment, get the hot work permit, set up screens, ventilation and fire precautions, and keep the fire watch.
Read electrode classifications, choose electrodes and filler rods, and store, dry, issue and record them correctly.
Check the supply, the machine and its duty cycle, the cables, the return path, the polarity and the VRD at every station.
Move and secure cylinders; fit and check regulators, flashback arrestors, non-return valves and hoses; set pressures, leak test, purge, light and shut down.
Work out bevel sizes, cut and clean joints, set the gap and alignment, have joints tacked to the WPS and inspect them with gauges.
Preheat and control interpass temperature when the WPS says, and plan tacking, pre-setting and the welding sequence.
Record fit-up checks, consumable batches and preheat, close the permit, and hand over unfinished work clearly.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on procedures and qualifications, consumables, arc and gas set-up, gas cylinders, joint preparation and its calculations, fit-up inspection, preheat, distortion, hot work and records.

A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as PQR, WPQ, acetone, quiver, open-circuit voltage, neutral flame, line-up clamp, valve cap) and essays that explain a procedure, a set-up or a plan in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** done as a team: preparing and inspecting a plate fit-up and a pipe fit-up to a WPS, and planning and setting up a shared oxy-acetylene and MMAW area under a hot work permit, with a toolbox talk.

blocks.note: In the essays, many marks are for the **reasons**. For each thing you check or set, say what goes wrong if it is not done.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Codes, the WPS and welder qualifications

blocks.p: A **code** is a published set of rules for a kind of work, such as the AWS structural welding code for steel. A **specification** is the client's or engineer's document for one job: it names the code and adds its own requirements. Together they decide how welds must be made, tested and inspected. Your Centre works to particular AWS codes and procedures, and your instructor will tell you which.

head: Document
What it is
How it is used
rows: Written instructions for making one kind of weld so that it meets the code: the recipe
The welder follows it; the team leader prepares the joint and issues consumables to it; the inspector checks against it
The record of a test weld made to the draft procedure, with the real settings used and the results of the tests on it, such as tensile and bend tests
It proves the WPS works. It is kept on file and shown to the inspector or client
The record that a named welder passed a test with one process, in one position, within set ranges of material, thickness and electrode
The team leader checks it before giving the welder coded work

blocks.note: The WPS says **how** to weld. The PQR proves that **the procedure** works. The WPQ proves that **the welder** can do it. A coded weld needs all three.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Item
What it gives
rows: Material specification or grade, and the thickness range the WPS covers
MMAW, OAW, GMAW, FCAW, GTAW or SAW; manual or mechanised
Joint type, groove angle, root face, root gap, backing and back gouging, often with a sketch and tolerances
Classification (such as E7018), size for each pass, storage and drying
Current type and polarity, and current and voltage ranges for each pass
Shielding gas, or fuel gas and oxygen, with flows or pressures and nozzle size
Minimum preheat, maximum interpass temperature, and where and how they are measured
Stringer or weave, number and order of passes, travel speed, cleaning between passes
Temperature and time, where it is needed

blocks.h: Using the WPS as team leader

flow: Get the correct WPS for each joint, at its current revision, and check that it is approved
Read it through and list what it needs: joint preparation, consumables, settings, preheat, positions
Check each welder's WPQ record against the process, position, material, thickness and date
Prepare and inspect the joints within the WPS ranges
Issue only the consumables the WPS names, from proper storage
Keep the WPS at the work place and brief the team on it
Record what was actually used: welder, consumable batches, preheat, problems

ul: **Process:** a welder qualified for MMAW is not qualified for OAW, FCAW or any other process.
**Position:** the test position decides which positions the welder may weld in production. A test in a harder position covers some easier ones, as the code's table shows.
**Material and thickness:** the test covers a range of thicknesses (and pipe diameters) and certain material groups, not everything.
**Electrode group:** for MMAW, a test with one group of electrodes (for example low-hydrogen) covers that group and some others, as the code's table says.

**In date:** the qualification stays in force only while the welder keeps using the process. Under many AWS codes this is shown in a **continuity log** at least every six months. If the welder has not used the process for longer, or his work gives a reason to doubt it, he must be retested.

blocks.note: If a welder's record does not cover the job, do not let him weld it 'just this once'. Give him other work or arrange a test. A weld made by an unqualified welder can be rejected however good it looks.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: AWS positions are a number and a letter: **G** for a groove (butt) weld and **F** for a fillet weld. The ISO system uses letters. Drawings and WPSs in Jamaica use either, so learn both.

head: AWS
ISO
What it is
rows: Flat: welded from above, with the weld face upward
Horizontal fillet: one plate flat, one upright, welded in the corner from above
Horizontal butt: plates upright, weld axis horizontal
Pipe fixed with its axis horizontal; the welder works round it
Pipe fixed with its axis at 45°; the hardest common pipe test
Pipe turned on rollers so the weld is always made on top

blocks.note: A **6G** pipe test covers most production positions, because the welder meets flat, vertical, horizontal and overhead welding in one joint. A **3G** plate test, under the usual AWS structural tables, covers flat, horizontal and vertical plate work but not overhead.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Planning the job and choosing the process

head: Point
Oxy-acetylene welding (OAW)
MMAW
rows: A soft, spread flame; slow to heat; wide heat-affected zone
An intense arc; fast; narrow heat-affected zone
Thin sheet and small pipe, about 0.8–3 mm
About 3 mm upward; thick plate in several passes
Gas cylinders only: no electricity needed
Mains power or an engine-driven welder
Slow; heats a wide area, so plate distorts more
Other uses of the same set
Cutting, heating, bending, brazing, bronze welding
Too slow and too hot for structural plate; cylinders to handle and store
Easy to burn through thin sheet; slag and spatter; needs a power source

blocks.p: Choose the process from the job: the material and its thickness, the position, where the work is (shop or site, with or without power), what the code and the WPS allow, the welders' qualifications, and the equipment you have. On a coded job the WPS has already fixed the process: you prepare for what it says.

ul: A 1.2 mm sheet-metal duct repair: OAW (or GTAW), because MMAW would burn through.
A 10 mm base frame for a pump: MMAW, because OAW is slow and its wide heat distorts plate.
A gate post on a hillside with no supply: an engine-driven MMAW welder, or OAW if the steel is thin.
Thick structural plate to a code: MMAW with low-hydrogen electrodes (or another process where the shop has it), exactly as the WPS says.
Brazing a copper or brass fitting: the oxy-acetylene set, with the right rod and flux.

blocks.p: Before a team starts a job, write a short plan, so that everyone works from the same facts. It should list:

ul: The drawing and WPS numbers, and the joints to be prepared
The joint sizes worked out from the WPS: bevel depth and width, root face, gap
The materials, with grades and heat numbers to check against their certificates
The consumables, and how they will be stored and issued
The equipment, tools and gauges, including temperature crayons
The preheat and how it will be checked
The hazards, the controls and the permits needed
Who does what, and who checks and signs off

blocks.p: A **toolbox talk** is a short briefing (often 5–10 minutes) at the work place before a job or a shift. Its purpose is that everyone knows the hazards, the controls, the plan and their own role, and has had the chance to ask questions.

flow: The job: what we are doing today, and to which WPS
The hazards: for example acetylene, arc light, fire, fumes, heavy plate
The controls: permit conditions, PPE, screens, extinguishers, fire watch
The roles: who sets up, who welds, who inspects, who keeps the fire watch
The emergency plan: extinguishers and exits, how to shut off the gas, who calls for help
Questions; then everyone signs the talk record

blocks.note: Dial **110** for the fire brigade and ambulance and **119** for the police. Put these numbers and the address of the site on the permit and in the toolbox talk, so nobody has to think about them in an emergency.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Work often stops with joints fitted but not welded, or half welded. The next shift must not have to guess. A **handover record** gives, for each joint: its fit-up inspection result and who signed it, the WPS, the consumables and batches issued, the preheat needed and whether it was reached, which passes are done, and anything still to check. Unfinished joints on a coded job are labelled, and low-hydrogen electrodes go back into the oven.

sections.title: The work area, hot work and leading safely

blocks.p: Oxy-acetylene and MMAW together bring most of the workshop's serious hazards into one place: fuel gas and oxygen under pressure, flames, arc light, electricity, fumes, sparks, hot metal and heavy plate. As team leader you plan the controls before the job starts, and you check that they stay in place.

head: Hazard
Where it comes from
Controls
rows: Sparks, slag and flames; acetylene leaks; containers that held fuel; grease in ducts
Leaking oxygen hoses or fittings; oxygen used to 'freshen' air or blow dust off clothes
Never use oxygen for ventilation or cleaning
Cylinder valves shut when not in use
No oil or grease on oxygen fittings
MMAW machines, holders and cables, worst in damp places and inside steel tanks
The arc (ultraviolet and infrared); the gas flame (bright light and infrared)
Electrode coatings, coatings on the steel, flame gases in enclosed spaces
Hot plate, slag and preheated joints

head: Work
Typical filter shade
rows: Gas welding of heavier work, and heating

blocks.note: These are typical figures from shade charts: follow the chart and your instructor. Gas-welding shades **do not** protect the eyes from an electric arc. Where OAW and MMAW share an area, screen the arcs so the gas welders and helpers are not flashed.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **hot work permit** is written permission to weld, cut, braze or grind where there is a fire risk. An authorised person issues it only after the area has been checked, and it sets the conditions and a time limit. Bays that are built for hot work may not need one; work anywhere else, and wherever the Centre's or the client's rules say, does.

flow: Plan: look at the job and the area, and do the risk assessment
Apply: request the permit from the authorised person, with the job, place, time and controls
Prepare: remove or cover combustibles, cover gaps in floors and walls, protect or isolate gas and fuel lines, set up screens, extinguishers and ventilation
Issue: the issuer checks the area and signs; the team leader explains the conditions to the team
Work: keep to the conditions and the time; stop if anything changes, such as a gas smell or another trade arriving
Fire watch: keep watching the area for the time the permit sets after hot work stops (often 30–60 minutes)
Close: inspect the area, sign the permit off, return it, and file the record

blocks.note: If the permit runs out, or one of its conditions can no longer be met, **hot work stops**. The issuer must check the area again and renew or reissue the permit before work restarts.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Inside a steel tank, pipe or boiler, the welder's body touches the work, and sweat or condensation makes shock far more likely. Use dry PPE, insulating mats, a machine with a working VRD, and keep the machine and the gas cylinders **outside** the space.

Never take gas cylinders into a confined space. Take the torch and hoses in only when work starts, and out again at every break: a leak while nobody is there can fill the space with fuel gas or oxygen.
A confined space needs its own permit, an air test, ventilation, a rescue plan and a standby person outside.

blocks.note: Oxygen does not burn, but it makes everything else burn far more fiercely. Clothing that has soaked up oxygen can burst into flame from one spark. **Never** use oxygen to blow dust off clothes or to freshen the air in a tank.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Check every station's set-up yourself before work starts, not just your own.
Stop work that is unsafe, explain why, and put it right before restarting.
Protect people who are not welding (helpers, other trades, visitors) from arc light and sparks.
Report and record injuries, near misses and damaged equipment.

blocks.p: Consumables must be the type the WPS names, in good condition, stored correctly and traceable. As team leader you choose them where the WPS allows a choice, check them on delivery, and control how they are stored and issued.
Carbon steel electrodes are classified by the American Welding Society (AWS) system, as in E7018. Many packets also carry the ISO classification.

head: Part
What it means
E7018
E6013
E6010
rows: Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal, in thousands of psi
Positions: 1 = all positions; 2 = flat and horizontal fillet only; 4 = flat, horizontal, overhead and vertical down
Type of coating and the current it runs on
18: low hydrogen with iron powder; AC or DCEP
13: rutile; AC or DC of either polarity

blocks.p: Letters after the code tell you more. **H4** or **H8** means the weld metal holds no more than about 4 or 8 ml of diffusible hydrogen per 100 g: the lower the number, the lower the risk of hydrogen cracking. **R** means the coating resists picking up moisture. **-1** after E7018 shows improved impact toughness.

head: Type
Example
Strong points
Weak points
Typical use
rows: Easy to strike and restart; smooth, neat bead; slag lifts easily; runs on AC
Higher hydrogen; lower toughness; light penetration
General light fabrication, thin sections, non-coded work
Low hydrogen; tough, crack-resistant, strong weld metal
Must be kept dry in an oven; needs a short arc; harder to restart
Structural steel; thick or restrained joints; higher-carbon steels; coded work
Deep, digging arc; fast-freezing pool; good for open roots and downhill pipe welding
Pipe root passes, pipelines, site work

head: Electrode
Before opening
After opening
If it gets damp
rows: In a **holding oven**, often about 120–150 °C; on site in a heated **quiver**; back in the oven at breaks and at the end of the shift
Re-dry (re-bake) as the maker says, often about 350 °C for 1–2 hours, and only as many times as the maker allows; otherwise scrap
Sealed; used straight from the pack
Used within the time the maker gives, then into the oven or re-baked as the maker says
Dry store or a warm cabinet
Dry at the low temperature on the packet, never at E7018 temperatures
In the closed packet or tin, at room temperature
**Never bake**: the coating needs a little moisture to work, and baking spoils it

blocks.note: Jamaica's humid air, worst in the rainy seasons (roughly May–June and September–November), soaks electrode coatings quickly. An E7018 electrode left on a bench overnight is re-dried as the maker says, or scrapped; it is never used on a coded joint because it is 'only a little damp'.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: On a site with no supply for an oven, many engine-driven welders have auxiliary power outlets that can run a portable rod oven. Issue low-hydrogen electrodes in small amounts and keep the rest sealed or heated.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Filler rods and fluxes for gas work

ul: Mild steel gas-welding rods are usually **copper-coated** to stop rust in storage. Choose the rod diameter from the chart for the thickness and technique (for leftward welding, a common guide is about half the plate thickness plus 1 mm).
Brazing and bronze-welding rods need a **flux** that suits the rod and the metal, to clean the joint and keep it clean. Keep flux tins closed and dry.
Keep rods in labelled tubes showing the classification and batch. Set aside unlabelled rods.

blocks.p: On a coded job every consumable must be traceable. Write the electrode classification, size and **batch (lot) number** on the weld record for each joint, and keep the maker's certificate on file. If a batch is later found to be faulty, the records show exactly which welds used it.

ul: Check deliveries: the classification on each packet matches the WPS and the order, and the certificates came with them.
Keep different classifications and batches apart, and labelled.
Issue from the oven in small amounts, recorded against the job.
Set aside and report any packet that is damaged, wet or unlabelled.

blocks.p: A team job may need several MMAW stations, in the shop or on site. Check each one fully: one fault at one station (a hot cable, a stray return path, a dead VRD) can injure someone or spoil a weld.

ul: Jamaica's mains supply is 110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz. Check each machine's rating plate (input voltage, phase and input current) against the outlets on the site.

Use outlets and circuits rated for the machine's input current, with the protection the Centre's rules require (for example an RCD on site supplies). Only a qualified electrician installs or alters mains wiring.
Long, thin extension leads on the mains side overheat and make the machine weld poorly.

Where there is no supply, use an **engine-driven welder**. Place it outdoors on firm, level ground, with its exhaust pointing away from people, doors, windows and air intakes, never inside a building, container or tank. Refuel only with the engine stopped and cool, away from sparks.

blocks.note: Engine exhaust contains **carbon monoxide**, which you cannot see or smell. People have died running generators and engine-driven welders in enclosed spaces.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The **duty cycle** is the percentage of a 10-minute period that a machine can weld at a given current without overheating. A machine rated 200 A at 60% can weld for 6 minutes in every 10 at 200 A. At a lower current the duty cycle is higher; at a higher current it is lower.
When the current you need is not on the rating plate, a common estimate is: **new duty cycle = rated duty cycle × (rated current ÷ new current)²**.

head: Example
Working
rows: Rated 250 A at 40%; job needs 200 A
Rated 180 A at 30%; job needs 150 A
Rated 160 A at 60%; job needs 200 A
60 × (160 ÷ 200)² = 60 × 0.64 = about 38%, and 200 A may be beyond the machine's maximum: check the plate

blocks.note: This is an estimate. Duty cycles are measured at a set air temperature (often 40 °C), so a machine standing in the sun on a Jamaican site reaches its thermal cut-out sooner. Plan each welder's arc time, keep machines in the shade with their vents clear, and turn the job's current down only within the WPS range.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Cables must be big enough for the **current**, the **duty cycle** and the **total length** of the circuit (electrode lead plus return lead). A cable that is too small gets hot, loses voltage along its length (**voltage drop**), and makes the arc weak and hard to control at the far end.

head: Total circuit length
Typical effect on cable size (a guide only)
rows: Sized from the current alone (for example about 35 mm² for up to about 200 A at a moderate duty cycle)
Usually one size bigger (for example 50 mm²)
Bigger again (for example 70 mm²), or move the machine closer

blocks.note: Use the cable maker's or the machine maker's chart. Unroll cables fully while welding, and lay them where they will not be driven over, tripped on or cut.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Fix the work return clamp on clean, bare metal **on the job**, close to the joint.

Never let welding current return through building steel, pipework, rails, chains, hoists, bearings or another machine's frame. Stray current can overheat chains and slings, arc across bearings and damage them, and give people shocks.
Where several machines weld one structure, each machine's return lead goes to the part being welded, near its own welder.

blocks.p: The **open-circuit voltage (OCV)** is the voltage between electrode and work when the machine is on and no arc is struck: often about 50–90 V. It is the voltage most likely to give a welder a shock. A **voltage-reducing device (VRD)** lowers the voltage at the holder to a safer level (often below about 35 V) whenever no arc is burning, and restores full OCV the moment the electrode touches the work.

ul: Use a VRD in damp, hot or cramped places, inside tanks and pipes, and wherever the Centre's rules say.
Test the VRD before use as the maker says; many have a lamp that shows it is working.
A VRD does not replace dry PPE and sound insulation.

blocks.h: Checks at each station before welding starts

head: Item
Check
rows: Rating plate suits the supply and the job; case closed; vents clear; controls work; in the shade, on dry ground
Undamaged; correct outlet; protection in place
No cuts, burns or bare copper; right size for the current and length; connections tight; safely routed
Jaws clean and firm; insulation whole
Firm spring and clean jaws; on clean metal on the job, near the joint
As the WPS says for each pass (for example DCEP for E7018); current within the WPS range
Screens, extinguisher, ventilation or extraction, dry floor, no combustibles

blocks.note: On a coded job the WPS gives a current **range**, and the dial on many machines is only a guide. Where readings must be recorded, measure the real current with a calibrated **clamp meter** on the cable.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Hazard
Why
Control
rows: Free acetylene can break down explosively if it is compressed above about 1 bar (15 psi)
Never set the working pressure above about 1 bar (15 psi). For a bigger flame, use a bigger nozzle from the chart
The cylinder is packed with a porous mass soaked in **acetone**, which holds the acetylene safely
Store and use cylinders **upright**, so liquid acetone stays away from the valve. If a cylinder has been lying down, stand it upright for the time the supplier says before use
Taking gas too fast pulls acetone into the regulator and hoses; the flame turns smoky and purple-tinged
Keep within the supplier's maximum withdrawal rate (often given as about one-seventh to one-fifth of the contents per hour). For big heating nozzles, connect several cylinders on a **manifold**
Acetylene reacts with **copper, silver and mercury** to form acetylides, which can explode with a knock
Never use copper pipe, or fittings high in copper (a common rule is no more than 70% copper); use only fittings made for acetylene
Acetylene burns in air at anything from about 2.5% to over 80%
Leak test every joint; ventilate; no naked lights near cylinders

ul: Oxygen cylinders are at high pressure when full (often about 150–200 bar). A broken valve can turn a cylinder into a missile, so fit the valve cap when moving it and keep it chained upright.
Oil and grease in contact with high-pressure oxygen can ignite violently. Never oil regulators, valves or fittings, and keep greasy gloves and rags away from them.
Oxygen enrichment makes clothing and hair burn fiercely (see the work area section).

Move cylinders upright on a **cylinder trolley**, chained, with valves shut and regulators removed or valve caps fitted. Never roll them on their sides, drop them, or lift them by the valve or the cap.
In use, keep them upright and chained to a trolley, wall or stand, away from heat, sparks and electric cables.
Store oxygen apart from fuel gases, by the distance or fire-resisting wall the Centre's rules give (a common rule is about 3–6 m). Keep full and empty cylinders apart and marked.
Leave the acetylene cylinder key on the valve while the cylinder is in use, so it can be shut at once.

head: Part
Its job
Check
rows: Outlet clean and free of oil; 'crack' it (open and shut quickly), standing to one side, to blow out dust, away from any flame
Reduces the cylinder pressure to a steady working pressure
Right gas and thread; gauges undamaged; adjusting screw wound **out** before the cylinder valve is opened, so full pressure does not slam onto the diaphragm
Stops a flame travelling back through it, and stops reverse gas flow; many also have a cut-off that closes with heat or pressure
Fitted at the regulator outlets (and at the torch where the maker says); in date; checked or replaced after any flashback
Lets gas flow one way only, so oxygen cannot be pushed into the fuel hose or fuel into the oxygen hose
Fitted at the torch inlets, or as the maker says
Fuel gas **red**; oxygen **blue** on international-pattern sets and **green** on American-pattern sets; no cuts, burns or soft spots; proper crimped fittings, never tape or wire
Fuel-gas fittings have **left-hand threads**, usually with a groove or notches on the nut, so they cannot be fitted to oxygen equipment; never force a fitting
Mix the gases and shape the flame
Nozzle size from the maker's chart for the job; seat and threads clean; torch valves shut and working

blocks.note: A **non-return valve** stops gas flowing backwards. A **flashback arrestor** stops backward gas flow **and** stops a flame. The torch end needs at least non-return valves; the regulator end needs flashback arrestors.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Cylinders upright and chained, valves shut; valve outlets clean and free of oil
Crack each cylinder valve briefly, standing to one side, to blow out dust
Fit each regulator to its own gas with the adjusting screw wound out; tighten with the correct spanner, never by force
Fit the flashback arrestors at the regulator outlets, then the hoses, the non-return valves and the torch
Stand to one side of the regulator and open the cylinder valves **slowly**: acetylene usually no more than about 1–1½ turns, with the key left on; oxygen as the supplier says (often fully)
Set the working pressures from the maker's chart for the nozzle
With the torch valves shut, brush approved leak-detection fluid on every joint; bubbles show a leak; shut off and repair any leak before use
Purge each hose on its own, one at a time, for a few seconds, in fresh air away from flames, to clear any mixed gas or air
Light the torch as the maker says (usually acetylene first, with a spark lighter), then add oxygen to set the flame

blocks.note: Never test for leaks with a flame, and never rely on smell or sound. Stand to one side when opening a cylinder valve: if a regulator fails, its front and gauges can blow out.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Flame
What it looks like
Uses
rows: A clear, rounded inner cone with no feather; about equal volumes of oxygen and acetylene
Welding mild steel, and most gas welding and heating
A white feather of extra acetylene round the inner cone
Some hardfacing and some brazing; on steel it adds carbon and can make the weld brittle
A short, sharp, pointed inner cone; a hissing sound; extra oxygen
Bronze welding and brazing of brass (a slightly oxidising flame cuts zinc fuming); on steel it burns the metal and gives a foamy, sparking pool

head: Event
What happens
What to do
rows: The flame goes out with a pop and may relight; caused by touching the work, an overheated or dirty nozzle, or too low a pressure
Shut the torch valves; find and correct the cause (clean or cool the nozzle, check the pressures); relight
The flame burns back inside the torch with a squeal or hiss; the torch gets hot
Shut the torch **oxygen** valve at once, then the fuel valve; close the cylinder valves; let the torch cool; find the cause before relighting
Flame travels back up the hose towards the regulator
Close both cylinder valves at once if it is safe. Take the arrestors and hoses out of use until they are checked or replaced; find the cause
Acetylene cylinder heated, for example in a fire
It can burst, even hours later
If it is safe, shut the valve; clear the area; call the fire brigade (110); cool the cylinder with water from a protected place; do not move it

blocks.p: Close the torch valves in the order the maker gives (many makers say fuel gas first, then oxygen). Close both cylinder valves. Open each torch valve in turn to let the gas out of its hose, then close it. Wind out the regulator adjusting screws, coil the hoses and hang up the torch. Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.

head: Term
Meaning
If it is wrong
rows: The angle cut on one plate edge
Too small: the electrode cannot reach the root, giving lack of side-wall fusion and trapped slag. Too large: wasted weld metal and time, and more distortion
The total angle between the two bevels; two 30° bevels give 60°
The flat left at the bottom of the bevel
Too thick: incomplete root penetration. Too thin: the edges melt away and the root sags
The space between the plates at the root
Too small: incomplete penetration. Too wide: burn-through, a sagging root and extra weld metal
A strip or ring under the root that supports the root pass
Must be the material the WPS says, fitted tight with no gap, and fused in

blocks.p: For a single-V butt joint:

ul: **Bevel depth = plate thickness − root face**
**Width of each bevel at the top = bevel depth × tan (bevel angle)**
**Width of the groove at the top = 2 × bevel width + root gap**

head: 16 mm plate, 30° bevel, 2 mm root face, 3 mm gap
Working
rows: Width of the groove at the top

blocks.p: Pipe is often bevelled at **37.5°** (an included angle of 75°), with a root face of about 1.5 mm and a gap of about 2–3 mm, as the WPS says. tan 37.5° = 0.767.

blocks.note: Work the sizes out **before** cutting and write them on the plan, so that the person bevelling and the person inspecting use the same figures. A tolerance written as 2.5 ± 0.5 mm means anything from 2 mm to 3 mm is acceptable.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Preparation
When it is used
Points
rows: Medium plate, or where only one side can be reached, as on pipe
Simple; but on thick plate it needs more weld metal than a double-V and causes more angular distortion
Thick plate that can be welded from both sides
About half the weld metal of a single-V of the same angle; welding the sides in turn balances shrinkage; the first root is back gouged
Tee and corner joints that need full penetration
Less weld metal than a V at large thicknesses, but costly to machine

ul: Cut and bevel by oxy-fuel cutting, plasma, a bevelling machine or grinding, as the WPS allows. Grind off the hard, oxidised skin that thermal cutting leaves, back to bright metal.
Clean the joint faces and about 25 mm each side (or as the WPS says) back to bright metal: rust, mill scale, paint, oil, grease and moisture all cause porosity, lack of fusion or hydrogen cracking.
For stainless steel, use brushes and discs kept **only** for stainless. Bits of carbon steel left on stainless rust and spoil its corrosion resistance.
Check the edges of thick plate for laminations (layers inside the plate) if the WPS or the inspector asks.
Set the root gap with spacers or gap gauges. On pipe, hold the ends in line with an even gap with a **line-up clamp** (internal or external).

Check **hi-lo** (the step between the two inside or outside surfaces) with a hi-lo gauge. Pipe is never perfectly round: if the hi-lo is over the limit, turn or re-align one pipe to share out the mismatch, and measure again. Never try to fill a step with weld.
Tacks on a coded joint become part of the final weld (or are ground out), so they are made by a **qualified welder** to the WPS, with the same electrode and preheat.
Make tacks small, sound and evenly spaced, with tapered ends so the root pass blends in. Grind out any cracked tack.
On pipe, use the number of tacks (often 3 or 4) or the bridge tacks the WPS allows.

head: Check
How
rows: Against the certificate and the parts list
Gap gauge, feeler blades or taper gauge
By eye, both faces and each side
Size, spacing, no cracks; made by a qualified welder
Right electrodes at the joint from proper storage; preheat equipment and temperature crayons ready

blocks.p: Record each result on the **fit-up inspection sheet**: the joint number, the values measured, the gauges used, the date and your name. On a coded job the inspector or supervisor signs it off before welding starts. A joint outside the WPS ranges is corrected and inspected again; it is never welded 'and made up with an extra pass'.
Hydrogen cracking needs **three things at once**:

ul: **Hydrogen** in the weld, from moisture in coatings, damp air, rust, oil, paint or condensation.
A **hard, brittle structure** in the weld or the heat-affected zone (HAZ), from higher-carbon or alloy steels, or thick sections that cool fast.
**Stress**, from shrinkage and restraint.

blocks.p: The cracks can appear **hours or even days** after welding, often in the HAZ, so they can be missed. Take away any one of the three and the risk falls.

head: Control
How it helps
rows: Low-hydrogen electrodes, kept in the oven and quiver
Less hydrogen goes into the weld
Removes the moisture, rust, oil and paint that add hydrogen
Slows cooling, so less hard structure forms and hydrogen has time to escape
Keeps the joint within the tested range: a minimum to keep cooling slow, a maximum to protect toughness
Post-heating or slow cooling, when the WPS says
Lets hydrogen escape before the joint is cold

ul: The WPS gives the minimum preheat. It depends on the steel's make-up (its carbon equivalent), the thickness, the hydrogen level of the process and the restraint.
Heat a wide band on both sides of the joint (often at least 75 mm each side, or as the WPS says) with a heating torch or electric heaters, so the heat soaks right through.
Measure on the parent metal at the distance the WPS gives (often 75 mm from the joint), on the side away from the heat where possible, after the heat has had time to spread.
Use **temperature-indicating crayons** (the mark melts and looks wet and glossy at the crayon's rated temperature, and stays dry and chalky below it) or a contact thermometer.
Tack welds need the same preheat as the main weld, because small tacks cool very fast.
On a humid morning cold plate can be wet with condensation. Even where no preheat is needed, warming the joint until it is dry and slightly warm drives off moisture that would add hydrogen.

blocks.p: The **interpass temperature** is the temperature of the joint just before the next pass starts. The WPS may set a **minimum** (often the same as the preheat) and a **maximum** (to protect toughness and, on some steels, strength). Measure it beside the joint before each pass. If it is above the maximum, wait for the joint to cool in air; never cool it with water.

Weld metal and the hot metal beside it shrink as they cool. The pull folds plates up (**angular distortion**), bows long members (**longitudinal shrinkage**) and pulls parts together (**transverse shrinkage**).

head: Method
How it helps
rows: Smallest weld and groove the drawing and WPS allow; double-sided preparations on thick plate; accurate fit-up with no oversized gaps
Set the parts out of line by the amount they will pull, so the weld pulls them straight
Weld equal amounts on each side of the joint, or of the member's centre line, in turn; or two welders working opposite each other at the same time
Weld from the centre outwards; use **back-step** welding (short lengths each welded back towards the last) or **skip** welding on long seams, to spread the heat
Clamps, strongbacks or jigs hold parts while they cool
Balanced tacks of the right size and spacing

blocks.note: Restraint stops distortion but locks in stress. A joint clamped too rigidly can **crack**, because the shrinkage has nowhere to go: this is worst in thick, hard or hydrogen-sensitive steel. Use only the restraint the WPS and your instructor allow.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: A distortion plan for a long member

flow: Reduce weld metal by joint design and accurate fit-up
Pre-set or pre-bend against the expected pull
Tack in a balanced pattern; fit strongbacks or clamps
Plan the sequence: centre outwards, balanced, back-step or skip on long seams
Check straightness and squareness at set stages, and record them
Adjust the sequence if the member starts to move

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what a WPS, a PQR and a WPQ record are, and how they link.
I can list what a WPS contains and use it to plan the preparation of a joint.
I can check a welder's qualification against the process, position, material, thickness and date.
I can name welding positions in the AWS and ISO systems.
I can choose between OAW and MMAW for a job and give my reasons.
I can write a preparation plan and give a toolbox talk.
I can explain how a hot work permit works, from planning to sign-off.
I can read E6010, E6013 and E7018 classifications, and the H4, H8 and R marks.
I can store, dry, issue and trace electrodes correctly, and say why cellulosic electrodes are never baked.
I can set up an MMAW station: supply, duty cycle, cables, return path, polarity, current and VRD.
I can work out a duty cycle at a new current.
I can explain the hazards of acetylene and oxygen and how each one is controlled.
I can assemble, leak test, purge, light and shut down an oxy-acetylene set, and explain arrestors and non-return valves.
I can set a neutral, carburising or oxidising flame and say what each is for.
I can say what to do after a backfire, a sustained backfire or a flashback.
I can work out bevel depth, bevel width and groove width for a single-V.
I can prepare, fit and tack a plate or pipe joint, and inspect it with gauges.
I can explain hydrogen cracking and how preheat, clean joints and dry electrodes prevent it.
I can measure preheat and interpass temperature correctly.
I can plan the control of distortion on a long member.
I can keep fit-up, consumable and handover records.

terms: Acetone
The liquid in the porous filling of an acetylene cylinder that holds the acetylene safely
Back-step welding
Welding short lengths, each one back towards the last, to spread the heat
Backfire
The flame going out with a pop, sometimes relighting
Bevel angle
The angle cut on one plate edge for a groove weld
Code
A published set of rules for a type of welding work
Continuity log
A record showing that a welder keeps using a process, so the qualification stays in force
Duty cycle
The percentage of 10 minutes a machine can weld at a given current
Flashback
Flame travelling back up the hose towards the regulator
Flashback arrestor
A device that stops a flame and backward gas flow
Heat-affected zone (HAZ)
Parent metal beside the weld that was changed by the heat but not melted
Hi-lo
The step between the surfaces of two pipes or plates at a joint
Hot work permit
Written permission to weld, cut or grind where there is a fire risk
Hydrogen cracking
Cracking caused by hydrogen, a hard structure and stress together; it can appear hours after welding
Interpass temperature
The temperature of the joint just before the next pass
Line-up clamp
A clamp that holds two pipe ends in line with the right gap for tacking
Manifold
A pipe that joins several cylinders to supply one torch
Neutral flame
An oxy-acetylene flame with about equal volumes of oxygen and acetylene
Non-return valve
A valve that lets gas flow one way only
Open-circuit voltage (OCV)
The voltage at the holder when the machine is on and no arc is struck
PQR
Procedure qualification record: the record of the test weld that supports a WPS
Preheat
Heating the joint before welding, to slow its cooling
Quiver
A small heated holder for low-hydrogen electrodes on site
Root face
The flat left at the bottom of a bevel
Root gap
The space between the parts at the root of the joint
Specification
The client's or engineer's document for one job
Toolbox talk
A short briefing on the hazards, controls and roles before work
Valve cap
A cover fitted over a cylinder valve to protect it while the cylinder is moved
VRD
Voltage-reducing device: lowers the voltage at the holder when no arc is burning
WPQ
Welder performance qualification: the record that a welder passed a test
WPS
Welding procedure specification: written instructions for making a weld to the code

c1.title: Pipe fit-ups for a pumping station near Bushy Park
c1.text: Kadeem is leading a team preparing butt joints in carbon steel pipe with an 11 mm wall for a new pumping station near Bushy Park, St Catherine. The WPS gives a 37.5° bevel, a root face of 1.5 ± 0.5 mm, a root gap of 3 ± 0.5 mm and a hi-lo limit of 1.5 mm. The root pass is welded with E6010 and the fill and cap with E7018. One trainee has put the E6010 packets into the electrode oven with the E7018 'to keep them all dry'. On the first joint the gap measures 4 mm at the top and 2.5 mm at the bottom, and the hi-lo is 2.5 mm at one point.

c2.title: Heating and bending at a training centre in Moneague
c2.text: Shanoya leads a heating and bending job at a training centre in Moneague, St Ann. The large heating nozzle uses about 1 800 litres of acetylene an hour, and the gas supplier says one of its acetylene cylinders should give no more than 1 000 litres an hour. During the set-up a trainee tries to screw the fuel hose nut onto the oxygen regulator and finds it will not turn. Later in the morning, a small flashback is stopped by the flashback arrestor on the acetylene line.

c3.title: Site welding for a warehouse frame near Montego Bay
c3.text: Garfield's team must weld the steel frame of a warehouse on a site near Montego Bay, St James. There is no mains supply yet, so the contractor has hired an engine-driven welder with auxiliary power outlets, and two inverters run from a generator. The welders will use 4.0 mm E7018 at about 160 A; the inverters' rating plates read 200 A at 35%. Rain is forecast for the afternoon, and the store with the electrode oven is 20 km away.

c4.title: A box girder for a footbridge in Falmouth
c4.text: Tamika is the charge hand on a 14 m box girder for a footbridge in Falmouth, Trelawny. The flanges are 25 mm plate. The WPS for the flange splices calls for E7018 H4R electrodes, a preheat of at least 80 °C measured 75 mm from the joint, and a maximum interpass temperature of 250 °C. The long web-to-flange fillet welds run the full length on both sides. It is a humid morning, and the plates stood outside overnight.

c5.title: A hot work permit in a hotel kitchen in Negril
c5.text: Dwight's team must repair a cracked steel bracket on a kitchen exhaust hood at a hotel in Negril, Westmoreland, with MMAW, and braze a copper fitting nearby with an oxy-acetylene torch. There are grease deposits inside the hood's duct, and the kitchen's LPG supply pipe runs along the wall 2 m away. The hotel's engineer issued the hot work permit at 11:30 am, valid for four hours. At 3:20 pm one weld is still to do.

questions.q: To the nearest 0.1 mm, how wide should the top of each bevel be? (tan 37.5° = 0.767)
o: 8.4 mm
7.3 mm
5.5 mm
questions.why: The bevel depth is 11 − 1.5 = 9.5 mm, and 9.5 × 0.767 = 7.3 mm. 8.4 mm forgets to take off the root face, 5.5 mm uses tan 30°, and 14.6 mm is both bevels together.

questions.q: What should Kadeem do about the uneven gap on the first joint?
o: Weld it, using a smaller electrode where the gap is wide
Weld it, and add an extra cap pass over the wide part
Accept it, since the average gap is close to 3 mm
Re-set the pipes until the gap is 2.5–3.5 mm all round
questions.why: The WPS allows 3 ± 0.5 mm, so 4 mm is outside it. The joint is corrected and inspected again before welding; changing the technique or averaging the readings does not bring a joint inside the procedure.

questions.q: The hi-lo is 2.5 mm at one point. What is the best first step?
o: Turn or re-align one pipe, then measure again
Fill the step with extra weld metal during the root pass
Accept it, because the cap pass will cover the step
Open the root gap to 5 mm so the root can bridge the step
questions.why: Pipe is never perfectly round, so turning or re-aligning one pipe in the line-up clamp usually brings the hi-lo within the 1.5 mm limit. A step that is welded over leaves a poorly fused root on one side, and a 5 mm gap breaks the WPS.

questions.q: Why must the E6010 electrodes come out of the oven?
o: The oven's heat softens the E6010 core wire
Mixing them makes the E7018 pick up moisture
Baking drives out moisture their coating needs
E6010 must be kept cold to stop it taking up damp
questions.why: Cellulosic electrodes such as E6010 rely on a little moisture in the coating for their forceful arc, so baking spoils them. They are kept in their closed packet at room temperature, apart from the low-hydrogen electrodes.

questions.q: What is the fewest acetylene cylinders that should be connected on a manifold for this nozzle?
o: One cylinder, with its valve opened fully
One cylinder, at a higher pressure
Two cylinders
Four cylinders
questions.why: 1 800 ÷ 1 000 = 1.8, so at least two cylinders are needed to keep each within the supplier's withdrawal rate. Drawing too fast from one cylinder pulls out acetone, and raising the pressure above about 1 bar is dangerous.

questions.q: Why would the fuel hose nut not screw onto the oxygen regulator?
o: Fuel-gas fittings have left-hand threads
The thread was dry and needed a drop of oil
The nut was cross-threaded and needs a bigger spanner
Oxygen fittings are metric and fuel fittings imperial
questions.why: Fuel-gas connections have left-hand threads (usually with a groove or notches on the nut) so they cannot be fitted to oxygen equipment by mistake. Never force a fitting, and never put oil on anything that carries oxygen.

questions.q: What should happen to the acetylene flashback arrestor now that it has stopped a flashback?
o: Keep using it, since it has just shown that it works properly
Turn the acetylene pressure up so a flame cannot burn back
Move it from the regulator end to the torch end of the hose
Have it checked or replaced as the maker says
questions.why: An arrestor that has stopped a flashback may be damaged, or its cut-off may have closed. It is checked or replaced as the maker says, and the cause of the flashback is found before the set is used again.

questions.q: Using the usual estimate, about how long in every 10 minutes can each inverter weld at 160 A?
o: About 3½ minutes
About 5½ minutes
About 4½ minutes
About 10 minutes
questions.why: 35 × (200 ÷ 160)² = 35 × 1.56 = about 55%, so about 5½ minutes in 10. 3½ minutes is the rating at 200 A, and 4½ minutes comes from forgetting to square the ratio. In the Jamaican sun it may be less.

questions.q: Where should the engine-driven welder be placed?
o: Outdoors on firm ground, exhaust away from people
Inside the site container, to keep it out of the rain
In the half-built store room, out of the sun and dry
On the truck, with a tarpaulin over the whole machine
questions.why: Engine exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which can build up to deadly levels in a container or room, and a covered machine overheats. It goes outdoors on firm, level ground with the exhaust pointing away from people and openings.

questions.q: With rain forecast for the afternoon, what should Garfield plan?
o: Weld faster through the rain so the joints are finished
Turn the current down so the wet electrodes do not spatter
Stop arc welding when it rains; cover joints and machines
Keep welding, but have the welders wear rubber boots
questions.why: Rain soaks PPE and the ground, making shock far more likely, and wet joints add hydrogen to the weld. Arc welding stops, joints and machines are covered, and work restarts only when everything is dry and checked.

questions.q: How should the E7018 electrodes be kept on this site?
o: In their opened box, in the shade under the truck
In portable ovens run from the welder's power
Wrapped in a plastic bag with the day's supply
In the sun, so that the heat keeps them dry
questions.why: Low-hydrogen electrodes must stay in a heated oven or quiver once opened. The engine-driven welder's auxiliary outlets can power portable rod ovens, so electrodes are issued in small amounts and the rest stay heated.

questions.q: Where and when should the preheat be checked?
o: On the joint face, as the torch is taken away
At the far end of the flange, its coolest part
By hand, when the steel is too hot to touch
75 mm from the joint, once the heat has spread
questions.why: The WPS sets where the temperature is measured. The surface the flame has just heated reads falsely high, so the heat is given time to soak through and the reading is taken 75 mm from the joint with a crayon or contact thermometer.

questions.q: Before the next pass on a splice, the contact thermometer reads 290 °C. What should happen?
o: Weld the next pass at once while it is hot
Cool the joint with water to save time
Turn the current down and carry on welding
Wait for it to cool in air to below 250 °C
questions.why: The maximum interpass temperature protects the toughness of the weld and the HAZ. The joint is left to cool in air to below 250 °C (but not below the minimum preheat); quenching with water can crack it.

questions.q: What does the H4 in E7018 H4R tell Tamika?
o: The electrode is for the 4G overhead position
The weld metal is very low in hydrogen
The electrode may be re-baked up to four times
The electrode is 4 mm in diameter
questions.why: H4 means no more than about 4 ml of diffusible hydrogen per 100 g of weld metal. Low hydrogen, with preheat, is what keeps hydrogen cracking out of thick, restrained flange splices.

questions.q: Which way of welding the long web-to-flange fillets will best keep the girder straight?
o: One welder, running each fillet from end to end in one go
Weld the whole of one side first, then the whole other side
Two welders, one each side, working from the middle out
One welder starting at each end, meeting in the middle
questions.why: Welding both sides at the same time balances the shrinkage, and working from the centre outwards lets the ends move freely. Welding one side first bows the girder towards that side.

questions.q: Before any hot work, what must be done about the grease inside the duct?
o: Have it cleaned out and the duct openings covered
Weld quickly, so the grease has no time to heat up
Keep a bucket of water by the duct in case of fire
Nothing, as it is inside the duct, not on the bracket
questions.why: Grease in an exhaust duct is a serious fire load: heat through the steel or a spark can light it, and duct fires spread fast. It is cleaned out and the openings covered before the permit is issued; water is the wrong thing to throw on burning grease.

questions.q: At 3:20 pm, what should Dwight do about the permit?
o: Finish the last weld quickly, then return it
Ask the engineer to check the area and renew it
Change the time on it, as nothing has changed
Carry on while the extinguisher is still beside him
questions.why: The permit runs out at 3:30 pm. Hot work may carry on only while a valid permit covers it, so the issuer must re-check the area and renew it before the last weld; nobody else may alter its times.

questions.q: What should be done about the LPG pipe 2 m from the work?
o: Have the hotel isolate it, and shield it
Nothing, since gas pipes are made of steel and cannot leak
Wrap it in wet rags and weld as fast as possible
Point the torch flame away from it while brazing
questions.why: A fuel gas line next to hot work must be protected: the hotel isolates it where it can, and fire-resistant screens or blankets keep heat and sparks off it. Leak checks before the work starts are part of the permit.

questions.q: Under the usual AWS structural code tables, which job does a welder's 3G plate qualification with E7018 NOT cover?
o: Flat butt welds on plate
Vertical-up butt welds on plate
Overhead butt welds on plate
Horizontal fillet welds on plate
questions.why: A 3G plate test covers flat, horizontal and vertical plate welds, but not overhead work, which needs a 4G test (or a pipe test that covers it). Always check the record against the code's table.

questions.q: A brass fitting is to be bronze welded with oxy-acetylene. Which flame is usually used?
o: A neutral flame
A carburising flame
A soft, yellow, smoky flame
A slightly oxidising flame
questions.why: A slightly oxidising flame forms a thin oxide film on the brass that cuts the fuming and loss of zinc. A neutral flame is for welding steel; a carburising flame would add carbon and smoke.
